facts.text: Today’s matinee is the Met’s 1,017th Tosca. The very first was on 4 February 1901.
evidence: Tosca (1017)
The premiere at the Metropolitan Opera was on 4 February 1901

facts.text: Host Ailyn Pérez knows this composer from the inside: she sang Puccini’s Mimì at the Met in 2016.
evidence: also sang the role at New York's Metropolitan Opera in 2016
In 2010 she appeared as Mimì in La bohème

facts.text: No overture: three loud, strident chords, Scarpia’s motif, then the fugitive Angelotti bursts in.
evidence: The opera begins without any prelude; the opening chords of the Scarpia motif lead immediately to the agitated appearance of Angelotti
three very loud and strident chords which open the opera and which represent the evil character of Scarpia

facts.text: Freddie De Tommaso made his Met debut this month as Cavaradossi, opposite Lise Davidsen’s Tosca.
evidence: In November 2024, he made his Metropolitan Opera debut in the same role, opposite Lise Davidsen as Tosca.

facts.text: “Recondita armonia”: wait for the sustained high B flat, as the sacristan grumbles a counter-melody.
evidence: Cavaradossi's "Recondita armonia" with its sustained high B flat, accompanied by the sacristan's grumbling counter-melody

facts.text: Tosca arrives on her own motif. She’s suspicious, but the music paints her devotion and serenity.
evidence: Tosca's arrival, signalled by her motif
Though Tosca enters violently and suspiciously, the music paints her devotion and serenity.

facts.text: The love duet “Qual’occhio” is Puccini at his most sensuous, with an almost erotic lyricism.
evidence: the sensuous character of the love duet "Qual'occhio"
an almost erotic lyricism

facts.text: Lise Davidsen won Operalia in 2015 and debuted at the Met in 2019, as Lisa in The Queen of Spades.
evidence: In 2015, she won first prize in the Queen Sonja Competition and first prize and audience prize in the Operalia competition in London
In 2019, she made her debut at the Metropolitan Opera, New York, in the leading role of Lisa in Tchaikovsky's The Queen of Spades.

facts.text: The sacristan and choirboys celebrate Napoleon’s “defeat”: almost the last carefree moments in the opera.
evidence: the sacristan returns with the choristers to celebrate Napoleon's supposed defeat provides almost the last carefree moments in the opera

facts.text: Scarpia enters on his menacing theme. Then the fugitive motif returns three times, louder each time.
evidence: after the entrance of Scarpia to his menacing theme
the "fugitive" motif recurs three more times, each time more emphatically

facts.text: Quinn Kelsey started in the Hawaii Opera Theatre chorus in 1991. His Met debut: Schaunard, in 2008.
evidence: began performing opera in 1991 as a chorus member of the Hawaii Opera Theatre
Kelsey made his debut at the Metropolitan Opera in New York City as Schaunard in Puccini's La bohème on 29 March 2008

facts.text: Te Deum: Scarpia’s lustful reverie is sung right alongside the swelling chorus, then he joins the prayer.
evidence: Scarpia's lustful reverie is sung alongside the swelling Te Deum chorus
He joins with the chorus in the final statement

facts.text: McVicar’s staging premiered at the Met’s 2017 New Year’s Eve gala, co-produced with the Bavarian State Opera and La Scala.
evidence: New Production, New Year's Eve Gala
Production David McVicar
A co-production of the Metropolitan Opera, Bayerische Staatsoper and Teatro alla Scala

facts.text: That distant gavotte? Puccini adapted a student exercise by his late brother Michele, so he could “live again”.
evidence: while in the background a gavotte is played in a distant quarter of the Farnese Palace
For this music Puccini adapted a fifteen-year-old student exercise by his late brother, Michele
his brother could live again through him

facts.text: Offstage, Tosca sings a cantata with the chorus, most likely Puccini’s own Cantata a Giove, a lost 1897 work.
evidence: Tosca's voice is heard with the offstage chorus singing a cantata
The cantata is most likely the Cantata a Giove, in the literature referred to as a lost work of Puccini's from 1897.

facts.text: News of Napoleon’s victory: Cavaradossi’s brief, ringing “Vittoria! Vittoria!” gives the torture scenes only partial relief.
evidence: Cavaradossi's brief "Vittoria! Vittoria!" on the news of Napoleon's victory gives only partial relief

facts.text: Puccini thought “Vissi d’arte” was a mistake. He considered cutting it, since it held up the action.
evidence: yet was regarded by Puccini as a mistake; he considered eliminating it since it held up the action

facts.text: Met music director Yannick Nézet-Séguin conducts. In August 2024 the Met extended his contract through 2029–30.
evidence: In August 2024, the Metropolitan Opera announced the extension of Nézet-Séguin's contract as its music director through the 2029–2030 season.
Conductor Yannick Nézet-Séguin

facts.text: “All Rome trembled before him”: Tosca delivers it on one note, a middle C-sharp monotone, sometimes simply spoken.
evidence: "E avanti a lui tremava tutta Roma!" ("All Rome trembled before him"), sung on a middle C♯ monotone (sometimes spoken)

facts.text: Act III opens with a 16-bar horn theme. Remember it: the lovers will sing it in their final duet.
evidence: An introductory 16-bar theme for the horns will later be sung by Cavaradossi and Tosca in their final duet.

facts.text: These matins bells were researched: Puccini went to Castel Sant’Angelo to hear how they sound from its ramparts.
evidence: He journeyed to Rome and went to the Castel Sant'Angelo to measure the sound of matins bells there, as they would be heard from its ramparts.

facts.text: De Tommaso grew up hearing Pavarotti in his family’s restaurant. Pavarotti’s last stage role: Cavaradossi, here, in 2004.
evidence: his father played recordings by Luciano Pavarotti at the family's Italian restaurant
Pavarotti's last stage performance was as Cavaradossi at the Met, on 13 March 2004.

facts.text: A somber clarinet solo opens “E lucevan le stelle”, in B minor.
evidence: The aria is introduced by a somber clarinet solo.
Written in B minor

facts.text: Puccini insisted on the words “muoio disperato” (I die in despair), and declined advice to bin the aria.
evidence: 'muoio disperato' (I die in despair)
Puccini insisted on the inclusion of these words
for declining expert advice to throw the result in the waste-paper basket

facts.text: Ricordi wanted a transcendent love duet here. Puccini’s defense: Tosca is busy teaching Mario to feign death.
evidence: did not equate with Ricordi's idea of a transcendental love duet
Puccini justified his musical treatment by citing Tosca's preoccupation with teaching Cavaradossi to feign death.

facts.text: The final bars: the “E lucevan le stelle” theme returns tutta forza, as loudly as possible.
evidence: the theme of "E lucevan le stelle" is played tutta forza (as loudly as possible)
